claims.text: The initial material is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with nominal composition TaVCrW.
Conventional EAM potentials are inadequate for representing the diverse liquid-phase configurations of the target alloy.
Replacing EAM references with a well-trained MTP will improve reference–DFT phase-space overlap in the liquid.
The proposed method replaces thermodynamic integration with free-energy perturbation.
An MTP with training errors below 1 meV/atom will reproduce the ab initio phase-space distribution of multicomponent alloys.
The MTP accurately captures the diverse atomic configurations sampled by the liquid more effectively than EAM references.
A small variance in MTP–DFT energy differences enables rapid convergence of free-energy perturbation.
MTP-FEP free-energy differences will agree with traditional thermodynamic-integration results within 0.5 meV/atom.
The MTP-FEP method will reduce computational effort by approximately 80% relative to the baseline.
The MTP-FEP method will provide approximately a 20-fold computational speedup.
Electronic excitation effects will produce a melting-temperature shift of 48–57 K relative to the original TOR-TILD methodology.
A density-of-states gap at the Fermi level causes an electronic Gibbs-energy shift.
Solid-state short-range order stabilizes the solid by approximately 2.4 meV/atom.
The short-range-order contribution corresponds to a melting-temperature discrepancy of approximately 25 K.
The proposed calculations apply at 0 GPa and 2000–2400 K.
A 12×12×12 supercell contains 3456 atoms and is proposed for MTP training and molecular dynamics.
The calculations use both GGA-PBE and LDA exchange-correlation functionals.
Temperature-dependent magnetic fluctuations are negligible over the stated conditions.
Standard GGA and LDA have binding errors for V and Cr that introduce uncertainty in comparisons with CALPHAD.
The baseline TOR-TILD methodology uses two EAM potentials and computationally expensive ab initio molecular-dynamics thermodynamic integration.

contradictions.description: An 80% reduction in computational cost corresponds to a 5-fold speedup at equal workload, not the stated approximately 20-fold speedup; a 20-fold speedup corresponds to a 95% cost reduction.
